title: The End of Thailand’s Long Stalemate?
gist: A teaser (paywalled body) framing Thailand's 25-plus-year contest between a royalist conservative establishment and a reformist opposition, with Bhumjaithai leader Anutin Charnvirakul now prime minister as of 2026—signaling that conservatives have finally won and taken over the state.

insights.claim: As of 2026 Bhumjaithai party leader Anutin Charnvirakul is Thailand's prime minister, which the article frames as conservatives finally winning and taking over the Thai state.
insights.speaker: Duncan McCargo
insights.so_what: A conservative-establishment consolidation of power sets the political-risk baseline for Thai policy, markets, and reform prospects.
insights.locator: How Conservatives Finally Won and Took Over the State

insights.claim: For more than 25 years Thailand's conservative royalist establishment and opposition forces have been locked in a struggle over the country's fundamental political order.
insights.speaker: Duncan McCargo
insights.so_what: Frames current events as the resolution phase of a multi-decade structural conflict rather than a passing crisis.
insights.quote: For more than 25 years, Thailand’s conservative establishment and opposition forces have been locked in a struggle for the soul of the country.

insights.claim: Thai royalists seek palace institutions insulated from criticism, a military licensed to intervene in political crises, deferential parties, and free rein to clamp down on actors who fail to toe the line.
insights.speaker: Duncan McCargo
insights.so_what: Defines the establishment's governing preferences—useful for reading how a conservative-run state will treat dissent and civilian control.
insights.quote: Royalists want palace institutions insulated from public criticism, a military licensed to intervene in times of political crisis, deferential political parties and politicians

insights.claim: Thailand's opposition calls for a constitutional monarchy, a military confined to barracks, a competitive party system responsive to voters, and checks and balances that do not unduly punish elected politicians.
insights.speaker: Duncan McCargo
insights.so_what: The reform agenda now on the losing side—its suppression signals the direction of Thai democratic backsliding.
insights.quote: The opposition calls for a constitutional monarchy, a military that stays in the barracks, a competitive party system responsive to the people’s wishes
